content: Clofazimine is associated with several drug interactions and potential adverse effects, particularly related to its impact on the QTc interval. Below is a detailed explanation of its interactions, adverse effects, and clinical considerations: Drug Interactions: 1. QTc Prolongation Risks: Clofazimine, when co-administered with other drugs that prolong the QTc interval, can increase the risk of serious arrhythmias, including Torsades de Pointes and sudden death. Examples include: Ceritinib, Clarithromycin, Adagrasib, Entrectinib, Fexinidazole, Glasdegib, Hydroxychloroquine, Ivosidenib, Lefamulin, Macimorelin, Pitolisant, Ribociclib: These combinations are contraindicated or should be avoided. If co-administration is unavoidable, frequent ECG monitoring is recommended. Azithromycin, Chloroquine, Citalopram, Crizotinib, Dofetilide, Doxepin, Escitalopram, Fostemsavir, Gadobenate, Gemifloxacin, Gemtuzumab, Gepirone, Gilteritinib, Lofexidine, Mavorixafor, Mirtazapine, Osilodrostat, Oxaliplatin, Ozanimod, Quizartinib, Selpercatinib, Triclabendazole, Voclosporin: These combinations require caution, therapy modification, or close monitoring with ECGs. Macimorelin: Causes a QTc increase of approximately 11 milliseconds. Sufficient washout time of QT-prolonging drugs is advised before administration. Fexinidazole: Avoid co-administration with potassium channel blockers or other QT-prolonging drugs. 2. Metabolic Interactions: Rifampin: Clofazimine decreases rifampin levels by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. This interaction applies only to oral forms of both drugs. Sodium Picosulfate/Magnesium Oxide/Anhydrous Citric Acid: Clofazimine reduces the efficacy of these agents by altering colonic bacterial flora required for drug activation. 3. Toxicity Modulation: Magnesium Sulfate/Potassium Chloride, Sodium Sulfate/Potassium Sulfate/Magnesium Sulfate: These combinations increase clofazimine toxicity via QTc prolongation. Preand post-colonoscopy ECGs are recommended for patients at high risk of cardiac arrhythmias. Adverse Effects: 1. Dermatological: Skin discoloration occurs in 75-100% of patients. Dry skin and ichthyosis are reported in 8-28% of cases. Application of oil to the skin may alleviate these effects. Rash and pruritus occur in 1-5% of patients. Photosensitivity, erythroderma, acneiform eruptions, and monilial cheilosis have also been observed. 2. Gastrointestinal: Common effects include abdominal pain, diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, and gastrointestinal intolerance (40-50%). Rare but serious effects include bowel obstruction, gastrointestinal bleeding, anorexia, constipation, weight loss, hepatitis, jaundice, eosinophilic enteritis, and hepatomegaly. 3. Ocular: Conjunctival and corneal pigmentation due to crystal deposits, dryness, burning, itching, and irritation occur in over 1% of patients. Diminished vision and maculopathy (bull’s eye retinopathy) have been reported. 4. Neurological: Dizziness, drowsiness, fatigue, headache, neuralgia, and taste disorders are possible. 5. Psychiatric: Depression secondary to skin discoloration has been noted. 6. Laboratory Abnormalities: Elevated levels of albumin, serum bilirubin, AST (SGOT), eosinophilia, and hypokalemia. 7. Other Effects: Discoloration of urine, feces, sputum, and sweat. Increased blood glucose and ESR. Splenic infarction, thromboembolism, anemia, cystitis, bone pain, edema, fever, lymphadenopathy, and vascular pain. Contraindications: Clofazimine is contraindicated in patients with known hypersensitivity to the drug or its excipients. Pregnancy and Lactation: Pregnancy: Classified as Category C. Clofazimine crosses the placenta, and infants born to mothers treated with the drug during pregnancy may exhibit deep skin pigmentation at birth. Lactation: Distributed in human breast milk. Avoid administration to breastfeeding women unless clearly indicated. Pharmacokinetics: Clofazimine is highly lipophilic and accumulates in fatty tissues and reticuloendothelial cells. It is taken up by macrophages throughout the body. The half-life is approximately 70 days at steady state. Excretion is negligible in urine, with small amounts found in feces, bile, sputum, sebum, and sweat. Administration: Clofazimine should be taken with meals to enhance absorption. Clinical Monitoring: Regular ECG monitoring is essential for patients on clofazimine, especially when co-administered with QT-prolonging drugs. Dose adjustments or discontinuation may be required in cases of significant QTc prolongation or adverse effects. This information is intended for educational purposes and should be tailored to individual patient needs. Always consult the latest clinical guidelines and drug formularies for updates.
